reading.body:
Nebius is building a 300 MW AI data center on 75 to 80 acres in Birmingham, Alabama, acquired for approximately 90 million dollars, with first-phase construction underway and full build-out targeted for 2028.

The facility represents a significant AI compute investment in a region without prior data center infrastructure at this scale. The project consolidates a former banking operations center with adjoining land, suggesting that repurposed industrial real estate can serve AI's power and thermal demands when paired with utility capacity. Alabama Power provides the electricity. The two-phase timeline, with a second 200 MW phase targeting fall 2028, indicates the developer's confidence in sustained demand beyond the first phase.

The project faced regulatory friction uncommon in data center development. Birmingham had a data center moratorium in place when the facility was planned. The city attorney determined in April 2026 that switching and substation equipment did not require city approval, effectively circumventing the moratorium. A resident class action filed in May 2026 names the city, the operator, and construction firm as defendants. This conflict between local governance and data center growth is not itself a compute constraint, but it signals the political friction that infrastructure expansion now encounters in population centers.

The 300 MW figure comes from secondary sources citing city proceedings, not from Nebius announcements. This is worth noting because it reflects how AI infrastructure planning now happens partly outside traditional corporate disclosure. The facility is modelled on Nebius's 75 MW Mantsala plant in Finland, indicating operational precedent but no published performance data specific to this site or operator.
